facts.claim: "It Takes Me Back" is a track on the two-song single "Broken Sky / It Takes Me Back" by Ray LaMontagne, dated August 25, 2023 and credited to Liula Records distributed by Mick Music. The track runs 3:41.
The Apple Music page lists "It Takes Me Back" with a July 28, 2023 date, ahead of the August 25 release of the full single.
Discogs credits Ray LaMontagne with writing, producing and engineering the single. He is also credited with vocals, acoustic and electric guitar, bass, piano, percussion and harmonica.
Discogs credits Carl Broemel on pedal steel guitar and Ariel Bernstein on congas for "It Takes Me Back". The listing spells Broemel's name "Broemet".

Discogs lists the single as recorded at The Big Room, mixed by Kevin Ratterman and Ray LaMontagne, and mastered by Kevin Ratterman. Its 7-inch vinyl release is on Liula Records (LR002), dated September 5, 2023.
The song features My Morning Jacket's Carl Broemel on pedal steel guitar.

Press coverage describes the song as being about LaMontagne's travels on the road. It uses pedal steel, harmonica and congas. His son Tobias LaMontagne (Zap Film Co.) made the single's lyric visualizer.
The song's opening lyric looks back on a life spent on stages, calling out changes to a pickup band and riding in a tired van that broke down in the rain.
The single came before Long Way Home, LaMontagne's ninth studio album. It was released August 16, 2024 on his own Liula Records and co-produced by LaMontagne and Seth Kauffman.
LaMontagne's 2020 album Monovision was his first entirely self-recorded album, with all instruments played by him.

LaMontagne worked in a Maine shoe factory before hearing Stephen Stills' "Treetop Flyer" on the radio. That song led him to pursue music, and his debut album Trouble (2004) was produced by Ethan Johns.

research.lineage: The song sits in the singer-songwriter folk and Americana tradition, and critics have long compared LaMontagne's raspy, soulful voice to Van Morrison, Nick Drake and Tim Buckley.

draft:
The best line in **It Takes Me Back** gives the landscape a better poker face than the narrator: "The countryside just shrugs and sighs," and then it looks the other way. Ray LaMontagne opens with a life spent calling out chord changes to a pickup band, in a tired van that breaks down in the rain. The hills don't care who passed through, and that indifference lets the song grow nostalgic without turning sentimental.

The sound fits a song about memory. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through an arpeggiated pattern. A bass holds a simple line underneath, and brushed drums keep a slow, steady pulse. The room sounds warm and open, the playing is polished, and no harmonies pad the vocal. LaMontagne sings low, with a rasp at the edges but a smooth line through the middle. That's the voice critics have tied to Van Morrison, Nick Drake and Tim Buckley for twenty years. He wrote, produced and engineered the single himself and is credited on most of the instruments. My Morning Jacket's Carl Broemel adds pedal steel, Ariel Bernstein plays congas, and press coverage notes harmonica in the mix too. It's singer-songwriter folk worn in like an old jacket. This is the Americana of a man who once left a Maine shoe factory after hearing Stephen Stills on the radio, and who has clearly spent the years since in vans.

The verses slowly pile up feelings the chorus won't settle. In the second verse the narrator runs from Utah toward Abilene and ends up in cuffs. He makes his defense in the same breath: no angel, just born free. That's self-justification and hurt in one shrug, and the song leaves both standing. The bridge is where the hurt comes through. Away and alone, he longed to tell her he was sorry, "But there ain't no turning back." That line quietly argues with the title. The chorus keeps saying the sound of wind through hickory takes him back to where he wants to be, but the bridge admits there's nothing there to return to. The light in her eyes went out "Like windows painted black," a hard, plain image of a house still standing with nobody looking out.

So the chorus is a comfort he knows is partial. He can go back in his head, but not to her. The single came out a year before *Long Way Home*, his ninth album, and the title fits the song.

The song sticks because it lets you feel nostalgia as a refuge and an admission at once: the place you most want to go is the one memory can reach and you can't.

factCheck.note: The lyric says "calling out the changes", not "chord changes". Changed to match. The van detail is supported.

factCheck.claim: Sings low, with a rasp at the edges but a smooth line
factCheck.note: Low register, gravelly/raspy, and smooth delivery are each backed by at least two passes.

factCheck.claim: He wrote, produced and engineered the single himself and is credited on most of the instruments
factCheck.note: Discogs credits writing, producing and engineering. Mixing was shared with Kevin Ratterman and other players are credited, so "himself" and "most" were overreach. Rewritten to list his credited instruments.

factCheck.note: He worked in a Maine shoe factory before hearing Stills' "Treetop Flyer" on the radio, which led him to music. The draft implied he left because of it, and the song title was missing.

factCheck.claim: Has clearly spent the years since in vans
factCheck.note: Unsupported. Replaced with the sourced point that press coverage describes the song as being about his travels on the road.
